articles.title: Watch: Warning of space arms race as US confirms weapons in Earth's orbit
articles.summary: The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale explains what an arms race in space might look like - and what it could mean for us on the ground.
articles.body:
The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities.

Russia and China responded by warning of an arms race in space.

However, according to the BBC's Defence correspondent Jonathan Beale, this is already happening.

Details of how the weapon operates have not been disclosed by US officials.

articles.title: 101+ Latino-owned brands to know and support in 2026 and beyond
articles.summary: Shop Latino-owned businesses selling clothing, hair care, beauty and health products. Celebrate the Latino community by supporting Latino-owned businesses.
articles.body: September through November is the busiest time of year for Melissa Gallardo’s candle brand Valorosa. Hispanic Heritage Month is from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15, and Dia de los Muertos — Day of the Dead — is traditionally celebrated on Nov. 1 and 2, so interest in Latino culture skyrockets during these months, as does the traffic to Gallardo’s site. With her candles encompassing nostalgic Latino scents like cafecito con leche, elote and lavender fabulosa, Gallardo’s mission is to celebrate Latino culture and put that representation on shelves. Latino-owned businesses are the fastest-growing segment of small businesses in the U.S., with over 5 million businesses owned by Latino/a entrepreneurs in the country, according to the Stanford Latino Entrepreneurship Initiative (SLEI). Though Latino business owners have solidified their role as strong contributors to American economic activity, they face a string of unique challenges compared to white, non-Latino business owners. “On one hand, the awareness around multiculturalism in all aspects of life — fashion, culture and food — is higher than ever,” says Maritza Abreu, founder and CEO of food brand Pisqueya. On the other hand, the enthusiasm for Latino culture hasn’t quite translated to more representation in other key markets, she says. That, paired with the lack of access to capital and difficulties staying true to core cultural values while maintaining a strong presence against larger competitors, makes being a Latino business owner both gratifying and challenging, says Abreu. Receiving support from shoppers is what allows Latino-owned businesses to continue thriving, and despite Hispanic Heritage Month amplifying these entrepreneurs’ voices, it shouldn’t just be one month out of the year, says Gallardo. “The contributions of the Hispanic and Latino community need to be celebrated year-round. I’m a business that celebrates Latinidad year-round,” she says. I connected with over 100 Latino-owned businesses, many of which are inspired by their heritage and cultivate a sense of cultural appreciation. The list of Latino-owned businesses below gives you a taste of the brands represented in sectors like skin care, home and kitchen and food. I verified that each company featured below is 51% owned by persons of Latino origin, akin to the way the Census defines Black-owned, AAPI-owned and women-owned businesses. Latino-owned beauty and skin care brands Ceremonia Inspired by the beauty rituals she grew up with, Babba Rivera founded Ceremonia to create more Latinx representation in hair care. “Despite us accounting for almost 20% of the population and being the highest spenders in many categories, hair being one of them, I kept asking myself, ‘Where are the brands that authentically speak to the new generation of Latinx folks, and more importantly, where are the category-leading brands founded by Latinx entrepreneurs?’” says Rivera. The Latinx community’s influence is present in all aspects of Ceremonia’s business model, including Ceremonia’s natural ingredients sourced from Latin countries, photographers, models and even the materials it uses in its accessories, says Rivera. The brand is thriving as a result: Ceremonia opened its first brick-and-mortar store in New York City last year, and became the first Latina-founded hair brand sold at Sephora. Daybird Daybird founder and CEO Whitney McElwain was frustrated by beauty brands selling the idea that in order to look and feel your best, you need to cover up your skin with layers and layers of products. Daybird started as a way to dismantle that standard with people of color at the forefront. “We look to create products with women of color in mind and create space for these same women on the shelf and in the media,” says McElwain. Its tinted skin care is what the brand calls a 4-in-1 multi-tasker: a serum, moisturizer and sunscreen all in one. While she’s proud to be a Latina entrepreneur, McElwain says it’s not easy to get small businesses off the ground. “Latinas less than half a percent of venture funding and this is deeply apparent in every investor conversation we have,” she says. This makes Hispanic Heritage Month even more meaningful to her. “For this one time a year, I truly feel seen.” De La Heart Gigi Vogel founded De La Heart after discovering the power of lymphatic drainage, which is a gentle massage that helps drain lymph nodes and targets the lymphatic system just underneath the skin. In 2019, Vogel launched The Body Tool and four body oils to help bring that ritual into people’s homes. Now, the brand has dozens of products across the beauty and wellness space, including dry brushes, body balms and butters, face and body sculpting tools, apparel and more. Kitsch Colombian-American Cassandra Morales Thurswell built hair and wellness brand Kitsch around an item most people use daily and often don’t think twice about: a simple handmade elastic hair tie. “That little accessory’s success showed me that hair care was so much more than shampoo and conditioner and inspired me to keep going,” says Thurswell. Kitsch has skin care, body care, sleep and shower essentials that are free of harsh chemicals, cruelty free and come in 100% recyclable packaging, according to the brand. Ocoa Beauty After years of using heat and chemicals on their curls and being told they had “pelo malo” (“bad hair”), Dominican Republic-born sisters Cory and Nicol Varona finally embraced their natural hair in 2017. Their curly hair journey involved learning how to treat and care for their curls, but they found most products out there were greasy, heavy and didn’t quite work — so, the sisters launched Ocoa (which is from the indigenous Taino language meaning “a place between mountains) in 2021 as a solution. The brand currently offers a four-step system for healthy curls: shampoo, conditioner, a curl-defining styling gel and a hydrating curl cream. Reina Rebelde While growing up in Mexico, Regina Merson’s makeup obsession started by watching her mom get ready and watching the telenovela “Rosa Salvaje.” Merson created Reina Rebelde as a way to reflect her identity as a Mexican woman living in the U.S. with bold, diverse and unpredictable shades and themes. You’ll find a range of makeup products inspired by Merson’s personality and fierceness, including contour kits, eyeshadow pallets, bold lipsticks and liquid eyeliners. Latino-owned clothing and accessories brands Eberjey Ali Mejia and Mariela Rovito cofounded Eberjey in 1996, a time during which the intimates market was very one-dimensional with designs made predominantly for the male gaze, according to Rovito. “There was a void for lingerie and sleepwear that are both sensual and comfortable,” she says. In addition to underwear and lingerie, the brand offers women’s and men’s pajamas, swimwear, loungewear and more. Ingrid & Isabel While expecting her first child in 2003, Ingrid Ocaña Carney, the Mexican-American founder of maternity brand Ingrid & Isabel, struggled finding a pair of pants that actually fit. That’s why she invented the Bellaband, a stretchy fabric that lets moms wear their pre-pregnancy jeans. The success of the Bellaband ultimately led to the creation of Ingrid & Isabel. More than 20 years later, Ingrid & Isabel is the largest maternity brand in the U.S., creating maternity fashion and postpartum essentials to support women from the moment their pants stop fitting through the third trimester and beyond. This year, the brand launched its new affordable, Walmart-exclusive line, Ingrid & Isabel For Every Belly. Little Words Project Adriana Carrig created Little Words Project as a way to create wearable affirmations and reminders of one’s self-worth and self-love in a classic friendship bracelet style. On the brand’s site, you’ll find pre-made bracelets with positive phrases like “Keep Going” and “You Got This,” and you can make your own bracelet with a custom saying. Min & Mon When Andrés Felipe Quintero and his wife Carolina Llano moved to the U.S. from Colombia, Llano wasn’t allowed to work due to her visa. So, she developed a fresh concept for unique whimsical and playful handbag designs, which became Min & Mon in 2014. “From that idea stemmed a dear desire to preserve the multigenerational leather tradition in Colombia that was disappearing for cheaper wages due to fast fashion,” says Quintero. Min & Mon offers a range of wallets, bags and small accessories. Nue After years of working in fashion, Stephanie Montes knew the secret to going braless under backless styles and plunging necklines was duct tape — but not only did it not look or feel great underneath clothes, it was a pain to remove. She created Nue’s breast tape and nipple covers to solve that problem for women of all shapes, sizes and skin tones. All of the brand’s tape — which comes in a 16.5-foot roll — is stretchy, hypoallergenic and available in four shades. Saalt Cherie Hoeger created period care brand Saalt with a mission to provide reusable period care products to those experiencing period poverty, fueled by her family in Venezuela not having easy access to period products while the country grappled with political instability. Six years later, Saalt has donated over 104,000 products that have reached more than 65,000 women and girls in need in 50 countries as part of its 2% give-back mission, which commits 2% of Saalt’s revenue to donating period care to regions with the most need, according to the brand. The brand has a variety of reusable period products, including menstrual cups and discs and leak-proof underwear. Springrose Shopping for an adaptive bra that her grandmother, who had chronic pain and arthritis, could easily put on by herself made Nicole Cuervo realize how few functional, stylish and size-inclusive options there were on the market. She began talking to women with a range of injuries, illnesses and disabilities, all of whom said they experienced the same issue her grandmother did. This inspired Cuervo to start Springrose, named after Grandma Rosa, and create the brand’s front-closure bras. Cuervo collaborated with rehabilitation centers to develop and test iterations of the bra before landing on its final design. “It means a lot to me that I get to work on a business that helps reduce pain and restore dignity and independence, while also creating jobs and opportunity for my community,” says Cuervo, noting that 33% of those who work with Springrose are Latinx. Latino-owned food and beverage brands Devoción Coffee Colombian-born Steven Sutton knows roasting coffee beans provides only half of the flavor — the freshness of the beans is what matters. Yet, most coffee beans sit around for months. So, Sutton launched Devoción in 2006 to produce the freshest coffee imaginable. The team hand-selects their farm partners, dry-mills at their Bogotá facility, controls the export process and roasts their beans in Brooklyn. Dolcezza Gelato In 2000, Violeta Edelman (who grew up in Argentina) and her husband Robb Duncan landed in Buenos Aires, Argentina after a three-month, 4,000-mile-long journey that started in the Brazilian Amazon. There, they discovered their passion for gelato — and thus the idea for Dolcezza Gelato was born. They opened their gelato factory in Georgetown in July 2004 without having ever made one batch, and now they offer more than a dozen flavors that include coconut with dulce de leche, peanut butter stracciatella and dark chocolate fudge. Pisqueya Maritza Abreu’s parents immigrated from the Dominican Republic and opened the doors to their Brooklyn restaurant, Puerto Viejo, in 1986. After a fire at the establishment, Abreu wanted to help her parents grow their business as they rebuilt it. She began bottling up family recipes and selling them as ready-to-eat sauces and seasonings, like Adobo, a blend of garlic, onion, salt, oregano, turmeric and black pepper. Pisqueya became a way for Abreu to share flavors that remind her of home with those beyond patrons of her family’s restaurant and help fill the gap in Latin Caribbean representation within the global food market. In addition to seasonings, the brand sells hot sauces and apparel. Siete Foods Veronica Garza founded Siete with her family after being diagnosed with multiple autoimmune conditions and overcoming major health issues. The family of seven (which is where the name “Siete” comes from) started learning about how certain foods affect health and a low-inflammation, elimination diet, which involves removing certain foods from your diet to figure out which ones can cause adverse reactions. A Mexican-American family from South Texas, the Garza family created Siete as a way to share authentic and healthy Mexican cuisines. The brand was acquired by Pepsi Foods earlier this year for $1.2 billion. Siete offers a range of grain-free Mexican foods, including almond flour tortillas, cookies and tortilla chips, as well as cooking sauces, seasonings, beans and more. Somos Somos was created by a group of three Mexican friends who felt there were not enough options for cooking authentic Mexican food at home in the U.S. They created ready-to-eat foods that capture some Mexican culinary traditions and authentic home cooking. The brand has oven- and microwave-ready rice and beans, entrees and burrito bowls, as well as cooking sauces, chili crisp and chips and salsa. Tia Lupita Foods One of the things Hector Saldivar missed most when he moved from Mexico to the U.S. in 2005 was his mother’s hot sauce. She began shipping him care packages filled with bottles of sauce, which Saldivar shared with friends and coworkers to teach them about his heritage. But Mexican hot sauce is not the same as what you find at American grocery stores, says Saldivar — it’s mainly made with peppers, while the primary ingredient in U.S. hot sauce is water or vinegar. “People kept asking me for more and more hot sauce, and I knew I had to find a way to bottle and sell this,” says Saldivar. Beyond the taste differentiating Tia Lupita’s hot sauce from its competitors, Saldivar says he made sure the product’s label, which features an image of his mother, helped it stand out. “Most hot sauces in the U.S. are very polarizing, very macho driven, and many communicate pain with skulls and bones and flames,” he says. “We use a label that communicates approachability and says our hot sauce is for anyone who is looking for some flavorful heat.” Saldivar says there’s currently so much excitement about ethnic food in the United States, specifically Mexican food, which has helped the brand “stick around” and continue growing. Beyond hot sauce, Tia Lupita now offers a line of tortillas, chips and salsa macha, a Mexican chili crunch. Latino-owned home and kitchen brands Bloomsybox Juan Palacio grew up surrounded by flowers in Colombia, the second largest exporter of flowers in the world after the Netherlands. After moving to the U.S. over 20 years ago, Palacio knew he wanted to share his love of flowers with others. In 2015, he founded the flower subscription brand Bloomsybox to not only help people discover different types of blooms year-round, but also to uplift his Latino roots by sourcing flowers that are mostly grown in Latin America. “I have noticed that customers are now placing a greater emphasis on brands that don’t shy away from their heritage,” says Palacio. “It’s not about impressing anyone, but rather embracing and celebrating one’s roots. I believe it’s crucial to embrace our heritage and share it with others.” You can subscribe to get Bloomsybox flowers monthly or weekly, plus choose your delivery date. Valorosa After Melissa Gallardo, founder and CEO of Valorosa (previously known as Bonita Fierce), realized the scents she grew up with weren’t represented in the home fragrance industry, she was motivated to create her own Latino-inspired candle brand in 2020. “Navigating language, culture and heritage has always been challenging but most of all, the feeling of what home means,” says Gallardo. “I set out to create a collection of Latina-inspired candles to share la cultura with the rest of the world.” She not only takes inspiration from her own experiences but also leans on community requests for scents that really encompass what it means to be Latino. However, starting a candle brand during the pandemic came with a unique set of challenges: On top of a glass shortage and increasing costs of wax and fragrance oil, it was tough to sell new scent-based products online without the in-person shopping experience. “I really had to hone in on my story and create a story behind every fragrance,” she says. Bonita Fierce After Melissa Gallardo, founder and CEO of Bonita Fierce, realized the scents she grew up with weren’t represented in the home fragrance industry, she was motivated to create her own Latino-inspired candle brand in 2020. “Navigating language, culture and heritage has always been challenging but most of all, the feeling of what home means,” says Gallardo. “I set out to create a collection of Latina-inspired candles to share la cultura with the rest of the world.” She not only takes inspiration from her own experiences but also leans on community requests for scents that really encompass what it means to be Latino. However, starting a candle brand during the pandemic came with a unique set of challenges: On top of a glass shortage and increasing costs of wax and fragrance oil, it was tough to sell new scent-based products online without the in-person shopping experience. “I really had to hone in on my story and create a story behind every fragrance,” she says. Now, Bonita Fierce is the first Latina-owned candle brand sold at Nordstrom, and this month, the brand launched nationwide at Barnes & Noble. Hedley & Bennett For over a decade, Hedley & Bennett has been known for its aprons. But Ellen Bennett, the brand’s founder and a native Angeleno raised by a single Mexican-born mother, has set her sights on more than just kitchen apparel as she and her team continue to grow the brand. “We want to bring the same level of quality to cutting boards, knives and other tools that we bring to aprons,” she says. “If you’re outfitting your kitchen, we want to be the brand you turn to now and in 50 years. How do we do that? We do it with great products.” Hedley & Bennett collaborates with a community of chefs to test the brand’s products during the research and design phase, and tweaks items based on the feedback it receives. “Nothing is ever done in a silo,” says Bennett. Latinx with Plants Latinx with Plants was created in 2019 by Andi Xoch and inspired by @blackwithplants, a community founded by D’Real Graham that celebrates and inspires people of color in the plant world. In addition to selling plants at its Los Angeles storefront, Latinx with Plants has plants, prints and merch available for purchase on its website. The brand also offers in-person pop-up events and plant workshops throughout the year. Loisa Loisa emerged after co-founders Kenny Luna and Scott Hattis created organic versions of the most famous Latin seasoning pair, sazón and adobo, so they can pass on their families’ Dominican heritage foods to their children without worrying about artificial ingredients and unnecessary fillers. In 2021, Dominican community chef and food activist Yadira Garcia of Happy Healthy Latina joined the brand as an owner. The name “Loisa” is an homage to “Loisaida,” the Spanglish name for Luna and Hattis’ hometown on the Lower East Side barrio of downtown New York City. In addition to offering pantry staples like seasonings and sofrito sauce, Loisa also has kitchenware tools and essentials, including mortars and pestles and a tostonera. Vela Negra Aisha Cort initially started Vela Negra as a stress-reducing outlet, and it soon evolved into unique candles and scents that capture Hamilton’s Afro-Cuban and Guyanese heritage. Cort, who is also an assistant professor of Latin American Studies and Bucknell University, says she pours candles with black wax because black absorbs and dispels negative energies, which helps inspire new beginnings and clarity. Each candle is individually hand-poured using 100% vegan coconut soy wax and ethically-sourced wooden wicks, fragrance and dyes. Latino-owned bookstores and educational brands Cafe Con Libros Cafe con Libros is a Brooklyn-based community bookstore and coffee shop that helps create a space where everyone, specifically womxn-identified folx, feel celebrated and affirmed. Owner Kalima DeSuze opened Cafe con Libros in 2017 as an intersectional feminist bookstore and an homage to her Afro-Panamanian roots. You can shop and pre-order books on the store’s website, along with merch and its monthly book subscription. Chau Luna Ximena Diego is an Argentine mother and journalist raising two bilingual children in New York City. To help bring up bilingual readers, she founded Brooklyn-based Chau Luna (which means “bye-bye, moon”) in 2016 to create a collection of Spanish-language books that children of all ages would enjoy. You can shop picture books, chapter books, audiobooks and more on the store’s website. Con Todo Press Naibe Reynoso, founder of Con Todo Press, is a Mexican-American multi-Emmy award-winning journalist based in Los Angeles, California. She created the publishing company in 2018 to create children’s books that celebrate Latino culture and help fill a gap in the publishing industry where women, Latinos and people of color are underrepresented. You can find the company’s Little Biographies for Bright Minds series, which are bilingual books that highlight Latina and Latino leaders, apparel, merch and more on its website. Duende District Duende District creates tiny pop-up bookstores all over the country for and by people of color. Each Duende District bookstore has a curated selection of new and used adult and children’s books by authors of color in English and Spanish. The bookstores partner with cafes and stores to open a literary space focused for communities of color. You can find Duende District locations in Albuquerque, New Mexico; Washington, DC; and Brooklyn, New York. You can shop the bookstore’s collection on Bookshop.com. Lil’ Libros Los Angeles-based bookstore Lil’ Libros was founded by two friends, Patty Rodriguez and Ariana Stein, who wanted to create a collection of children’s books that celebrate cultural diversity in English and Spanish. Rodriguez and Stein’s books aim to inspire young minds, ignite an interest in reading and help young people embrace bilingual literature. You can shop books, games and teacher resources on the store’s website. The Lit Bar The Lit Bar was founded by Bronx native and resident Noëlle Santos in 2019 after the last bookstore in the Bronx closed, leaving the community without a literary hub. It is currently the only brick and mortar bookstore serving the Bronx and is an accessible way for people to come together through social gatherings at the in-house wine bar and curated, local community programming. You can shop the bookstore’s curated lists on Bookshop.com. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m an editor at NBC Selected who has led the Identities vertical since 2021. For this story, I connected with over 100 Latino-owned brands and spoke to over a dozen leaders of the Latino business community to better understand their challenges and successes. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Why do some African leaders gamble with term limits?
articles.summary: Protesters in the DRC denounce law that could extend president’s term.
articles.body:
Already embroiled in a long-running conflict in the east and a rapidly spreading Ebola outbreak, the Democratic Republic of Congo risks plunging into further turmoil.

This time, the crisis is triggered by fears that President Felix Tshisekedi may try to serve a third term. But that would be contingent on a constitutional amendment and a referendum.

The parliament has passed legislation setting the terms for that referendum. It’s led to protests across the country and accusations of an attempted power grab.

So, what’s behind the president wanting to serve a third term? And what would the regional consequences be?

Guests: Kambale Musavuli – Political analyst at the Center for Research on the Congo-Kinshasa

Richard Moncrieff – Project Director for the Great Lakes region at the International Crisis Group

Oluwole Ojewale – Senior researcher for West and Central Africa at the Institute for Security Studies

articles.title: Cadu de Lula apresenta propostas para o governo do RN em entrevista | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato ao governo do RN participou da rodada de entrevistas nesta terça-feira (15) e apresentou propostas para diferentes áreas da administração pública.
articles.summary: Cadu de Lula defende reforço policial, ampliação da UERN e equilíbrio das contas públicas em entrevista sobre seus planos para o governo do Rio Grande do Norte.
articles.body:
O candidato ao governo do Rio Grande do Norte pelo PT, Cadu de Lula, participou nesta terça-feira (15) da rodada de entrevistas com os candidatos ao governo no Inter 1, na Inter TV Cabugi . Durante a conversa, ele apresentou propostas do plano de governo para áreas como segurança pública, economia e educação.

Na segurança pública, o candidato falou sobre o combate às facções criminosas e defendeu o aumento do efetivo policial para reforçar a atuação contra o crime organizado. Na educação, afirmou que pretende ampliar a Universidade do Estado do Rio Grande do Norte (UERN).

Cadu também falou sobre economia e apresentou propostas para manter o equilíbrio fiscal das contas públicas, além de garantir o pagamento de servidores e fornecedores em dia.

"A gente tem que saber equilibrar essa questão fiscal com os impactos sociais das políticas públicas. A gente tem compromisso com a trajetória do crescimento sustentável da principal despesa do Estado, que é a folha de pagamento, e também temos propostas para a questão da previdência, déficit previdenciário. A gente fazendo esse equilíbrio, porque o Estado já está nessa trajetória, a gente vai continuar nessa trajetória de melhoria dos indicadores fiscais, a gente vai ter cada vez mais recursos para investir e o Rio Grande do Norte vai poder andar com as suas próprias pernas".

articles.title: Operação em Montes Claros mira grupo que expulsava moradores de casa | G1
articles.standfirst: Ação foi realizada pelas Polícias Civil e Militar. As equipes prenderam duas pessoas em flagrante e apreenderam drogas, celulares e veículos.
articles.summary: Operação em Montes Claros prende suspeitos de integrar grupo criminoso que aterrorizava e expulsava moradores de suas residências no bairro Vila Telma.
articles.body:
Parte dos materiais apreendidos — Foto: Izabela Gonçalves/Inter TV

Um grupo que aterrorizava moradores e chegou a expulsá-los de suas casas em um bairro de Montes Claros foi alvo da operação Queda da Bastilha nesta terça-feira (15).

A ação foi realizada pelas Polícias Civil e Militar. As equipes prenderam duas pessoas em flagrante e apreenderam drogas, celulares e veículos.

Segundo a delegada Franciele Drummond, as ameaças começaram após um homicídio ocorrido em 4 de julho. Dois grupos rivais entraram em confronto e um integrante de um deles acabou morrendo após ser baleado.

"Depois desse homicídio, aumentou a tensão no bairro e várias pessoas ligadas a esse grupo criminoso começaram a ameaçar moradores, a coagi-los, expulsá-los de suas residências e a danificar residências como uma retaliação, uma represália a esse homicídio ocorrido."

O inquérito foi encaminhado à Justiça com indiciamento dos investigados e solicitação dos mandados de prisão.

De acordo com Franciele Drummond, foram cumpridos 11 mandados de busca e apreensão. Todo o material apreendido será periciado. Quatro pessoas são consideradas foragidas.

Sobre o grupo investigado, a polícia afirmou que os integrantes atuavam na Vila Telma e nos bairros vizinhos.

O tenente-coronel Lúcio Santos, comandante do 10º Batalhão da PM, disse que a corporação faz ações para garantir a segurança dos moradores e impedir o domínio territorial dos criminosos.

"O bairro Vila Telma, o Estado de Minas Gerais, a cidade de Montes Claros são governados pelo Estado, são governadas pelos pelas pelos órgãos públicos e pelas comunidades e não por grupos armados criminosos que praticam ações paralelas e de desordem."

O comandante ainda destacou que a população pode colaborar com o trabalho da polícia por meio de denúncias anônimas feitas pelo telefone 181.

articles.title: Pet hotel é condenado a indenizar família após cachorra desaparecer  | G1
articles.standfirst: A cadela de estimação desapareceu em 25 de dezembro de 2025 após o portão ser deixado aberto em um pet hotel em São José do Rio Preto (SP) e ainda não foi localizada. O g1 tenta contato com a empresa.
articles.summary: Um pet hotel de São José do Rio Preto (SP) foi condenado a indenizar a família tutora de uma cadela de estimação que desapareceu em 25 de dezembro de 2025 durante hospedagem.
articles.body:
Kika desapareceu há 1 mês em São José do Rio Preto (SP) — Foto: Reprodução / TV TEM

Um pet hotel de São José do Rio Preto (SP) foi condenado a indenizar a família tutora de uma cadela de estimação que desapareceu em 25 de dezembro de 2025 durante o período de hospedagem no local e ainda não foi localizada.

A decisão emitida em 10 de setembro deste ano pelo juiz Leonardo Lopes Sardinha estabeleceu que os proprietários do estabelecimento façam ressarcimento financeiro a três responsáveis pelo animal por danos morais, totalizando R$ 13 mil.

A Justiça também fixou a indenização de R$ 1.074,32 por danos materiais, tendo em vista que as vítimas tiveram custos com a impressão e distribuição de panfletos, contratação de carro de som e sistema de alerta, além de gastos com combustível durante o período de buscas pelo paradeiro do animal. Cabe recurso da decisão. O g1 tenta contato com a defesa do pet hotel.

Câmeras de segurança registraram o momento em que o responsável pelo estabelecimento tenta resgatar a cadela em São José do Rio Preto (SP) — Foto: Reprodução / TV TEM

A cachorra denominada Kika vivia sob os cuidados de uma mulher e de seus dois filhos. Em 24 de dezembro, a família viajou para Sorocaba (SP), onde passaria as festas de fim de ano. Kika e Neve, a outra cadela de estimação, foram deixadas no pet hotel.

No dia 25 de dezembro, os tutores foram comunicados pelo proprietário do local que Kika havia fugido.

Conforme a família, a fuga aconteceu porque o portão estava aberto e a cadela aproveitou a oportunidade para escapar. Câmeras de segurança registraram o momento em que o responsável pelo estabelecimento tentou resgatar a cadela, mas ela acabou fugindo. Assista abaixo.

À época, os tutores alegaram que a empresa não prestou assistência para localizar Kika e só fez um novo contato dias depois, devido à repercussão do caso.

Para divulgar imagens do animal, a família imprimiu e espalhou panfletos em São José do Rio Preto, além de usar as redes sociais para divulgar o sumiço, mas não obteve resultados. Quase nove meses após o desaparecimento, a cachorra não havia sido localizada.

Inicialmente, a família tinha solicitado uma indenização de R$ 60 mil à empresa. Entretanto, o juiz considerou o pedido inicial excessivo em relação ao porte do estabelecimento. O magistrado levou em consideração o luto e a dor pelo sumiço e pela perda da cachorra ao estabelecer as penalidades.

articles.title: Danone amplia produção em Minas Gerais e reforça aposta no mercado brasileiro | G1
articles.standfirst: Companhia inaugura nova linha de produção em Poços de Caldas para acompanhar demanda por alimentos proteicos e saudáveis, fortalecendo também a cadeia nacional de leite fresco
articles.summary: Companhia inaugura nova linha de produção em Poços de Caldas para acompanhar demanda por alimentos proteicos e saudáveis, fortalecendo também a cadeia nacional de leite fresco
articles.body:
Fábrica da Danone na cidade de Poços de Caldas (MG) — Foto: Danone

Em um momento de transformação dos hábitos alimentares dos brasileiros, com a proteína deixando de ser um consumo restrito ao universo esportivo para ganhar espaço na rotina de diferentes perfis de consumidores, a Danone inaugura em agosto uma nova linha de produção em sua fábrica de Lácteos, em Poços de Caldas (MG). A expansão reforça a capacidade da companhia para acompanhar o crescimento da demanda por alimentos proteicos e saudáveis, além de sinalizar sua confiança no potencial de longo prazo do mercado brasileiro, onde atua há mais de 55 anos.

"A nova linha representa mais um passo da nossa estratégia de crescimento sustentável no Brasil. Estamos ampliando nossa capacidade para acompanhar uma transformação de hábitos que vemos acontecer há anos: a proteína deixou de ser um consumo de nicho e passou a fazer parte da rotina alimentar dos brasileiros. Seguimos investindo em inovação, eficiência industrial e fortalecimento da cadeia produtiva local porque acreditamos no potencial de crescimento do país e das categorias ligadas à saúde e à nutrição", afirma Mário Rezende, VP de Operações da Danone Brasil.

O investimento está alinhado à estratégia da Danone de impulsionar categorias ligadas à saúde e nutrição, área em que a companhia vem desempenhando papel pioneiro no país ao longo de sua trajetória. A nova linha contribuirá especialmente para ampliar a produção de produtos de alta proteína, categoria cuja expansão reflete uma mudança estrutural no comportamento dos consumidores, cada vez mais atentos a emas como bem-estar, saciedade, longevidade e qualidade da alimentação.

A expansão da unidade de Poços de Caldas, que produz marcas icônicas como YoPRO, Danone, Danette, Danoninho e Activia, também reforça a estratégia da companhia de combinar crescimento dos negócios, inovação e fortalecimento da produção local. Nos últimos 10 anos, a Danone investiu quase de R$ 1 bilhão em suas operações industriais no Brasil e segue ampliando sua capacidade para atender categorias consideradas estratégicas para o futuro da alimentação.

Investimento industrial conectado ao campo

O fortalecimento da capacidade produtiva caminha em paralelo ao desenvolvimento da cadeia de leite fresco, principal matéria-prima da companhia. Por meio da Jornada Flora , iniciativa de agricultura regenerativa da Danone no Brasil, produtores parceiros recebem apoio técnico para adoção de práticas voltadas ao aumento da produtividade, à melhoria do bem-estar animal, à saúde do solo e à redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa.

“O crescimento da demanda por proteínas de qualidade exige uma cadeia produtiva mais eficiente, competitiva e resiliente. Com a Jornada Flora, mostramos que é possível aumentar a produtividade, reduzir emissões e gerar valor para os produtores de leite. A ampliação da produção em Poços de Caldas reforça essa visão e nossa missão de levar saúde por meio da alimentação ao maior número de pessoas possível”, afirma Camilo Wittica, VP de Assuntos Institucionais da Danone Brasil.

Atualmente, cerca de 60% do leite captado pela companhia no Brasil é proveniente de fazendas participantes da Jornada Flora. Desde 2020, o programa contribuiu para reduzir em 50% o fator de emissão de CO₂ e em 43% o fator de emissão de metano na cadeia de leite fresco da Danone. Além dos ganhos ambientais, a iniciativa gera, em média, retorno de R$ 116 aos produtores para cada R$ 100 investidos anualmente nas propriedades rurais.

Tecnologia para aumentar eficiência e reduzir desperdícios

A busca por maior eficiência e sustentabilidade também orienta os investimentos tecnológicos da unidade de Poços de Caldas. Uma das iniciativas implantadas na fábrica utiliza sensores de condutividade para identificar com precisão a passagem de água, mistura e produto ao longo das etapas de transferência nas tubulações industriais. A tecnologia permite otimizar processos, reduzir perdas de matéria-prima e aumentar a eficiência operacional. O projeto tornou-se referência interna e já é avaliado para aplicação em outras operações da Danone.

Outra frente de inovação é o uso de impressão 3D na produção de peças de manutenção. Atualmente, a unidade conta com 11 impressoras 3D utilizadas para reproduzir componentes plásticos empregados nos equipamentos fabris. Com apoio de scanners e softwares especializados, a tecnologia permite a fabricação de peças internamente, reduzindo prazos de reposição e aumentando a autonomia da operação.

Reconhecida como uma empresa B Corp , a Danone busca conectar o crescimento de seus negócios à geração de valor para toda a cadeia, desde produtores rurais até consumidores. Os avanços da fábrica de Poços de Caldas fazem parte da Jornada de Impacto da Danone , estratégia global que integra desempenho econômico, promoção da saúde, desenvolvimento de pessoas e comunidades e regeneração da natureza.

Recentemente, a companhia anunciou a segunda fase da Jornada de Impacto, estabelecendo metas até 2030 para avançar na melhoria contínua do perfil nutricional de seu portfólio, na expansão da agricultura regenerativa para produção de leite fresco, na redução das emissões ao longo da cadeia de valor, no desenvolvimento de competências voltadas para o futuro do trabalho e na promoção da inclusão de gênero e racial.

A Danone é uma empresa centenária global e líder no setor de alimentos e bebidas, atuando em categorias com foco em saúde, crescimento acelerado e alinhadas às tendências de consumo. No Brasil há 55 anos, atua nas categorias de Produtos Lácteos Essenciais & à Base de Plantas, e Nutrição Especializada.

Com uma missão de longa data de levar saúde por meio da alimentação ao maior número de pessoas possível, a Danone busca inspirar práticas alimentares e de consumo mais saudáveis e sustentáveis, comprometendo-se com impacto positivo em termos nutricionais, sociais, societais e ambientais.

A empresa definiu sua estratégia Renew para restaurar o crescimento, a competitividade e a geração de valor a longo prazo. Com mais de 90 mil colaboradores e presença em mais de 120 mercados, a Danone registrou vendas de €27,4 bilhões em 2024.

Seu portfólio inclui marcas internacionais líderes (como Activia, Danone, Danette, Danoninho, entre outras), além de marcas locais e regionais fortes (como YoPRO, Fortini, Souvenaid, Milnutri e Aptanutri)

A Danone está listada na Euronext Paris e também na plataforma OTCQX por meio de um programa de ADR (American Depositary Receipt). A empresa integra importantes índices de sustentabilidade, incluindo os gerenciados pela Moody’s e Sustainalytics, bem como os índices MSCI ESG, FTSE4Good, Bloomberg Gender Equality Index e Access to Nutrition Index.

A ambição da Danone de obter a certificação global B Corp™ foi concretizada em 2025. No Brasil, a Danone já é certificada como B Corp™ desde 2021, reforçando seu compromisso com práticas sustentáveis, responsabilidade social e transparência.

A linha Fortini foi desenvolvida para crianças com necessidades específicas e deve ser consumida conforme recomendação do profissional de saúde.

Souvenaid foi desenvolvido para pacientes com necessidades específicas e deve ser consumido conforme recomendação do profissional da saúde. O Ministério da Saúde Informa: O Aleitamento Materno evita infecções e alergias e é recomendado até os 2 (dois) anos de idade ou mais .

articles.title: PSI 2027 Ufam: Provas ocorrem nos dias 20 e 21 de setembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Ao todo, o processo oferece 636 vagas em cursos de graduação em cinco municípios do interior do estado.
articles.summary: Com 636 vagas em cinco municípios, o PSI 2027 da Ufam realiza provas neste domingo e segunda-feira seguindo o fuso horário de Manaus.
articles.body:
Ufam divulga edital de processo seletivo com mais de 600 vagas para o interior do AM — Foto: Foto: Carolina Diniz/Rede Amazônica

Os candidatos inscritos no Processo Seletivo para o Interior (PSI 2027) da Universidade Federal do Amazonas (Ufam) farão as provas no próximo domingo (20) e segunda-feira (21). Ao todo, o processo oferece 636 vagas em cursos de graduação em cinco municípios do interior do estado.

No domingo (20), será aplicada a Prova de Conhecimentos Gerais I e a Redação, das 8h15 às 13h15. Já na segunda-feira (21), os candidatos farão a Prova de Conhecimentos Gerais II, das 8h15 às 12h15.

Os portões serão abertos às 7h, e a recomendação da Ufam é que os candidatos cheguem com pelo menos uma hora de antecedência. Os horários seguem o fuso de Manaus.

As provas serão realizadas em Benjamin Constant , Coari , Humaitá , Itacoatiara e Parintins , municípios que possuem unidades da Ufam. Também haverá aplicação em Codajás , Manacapuru , Manicoré , Maués , Santo Antônio do Içá , São Gabriel da Cachoeira , São Paulo de Olivença , Tabatinga e Tefé .

Os candidatos devem apresentar documento oficial com foto e levar caneta esferográfica preta de corpo transparente.

Em caso de perda ou roubo do documento de identificação, será aceito boletim de ocorrência emitido a partir de 20 de julho de 2026.

O cartão de confirmação está disponível desde o dia 10 de setembro, e os candidatos devem conferir com antecedência o local onde farão as provas.

O PSI 2027 oferece 636 vagas distribuídas entre cinco unidades da Ufam no interior do Amazonas:

120 vagas para o Instituto de Natureza e Cultura, em Benjamin Constant, em seis cursos;

117 vagas para o Instituto de Saúde e Biotecnologia, em Coari, em sete graduações;

150 vagas para o Instituto de Educação, Agricultura e Ambiente, em Humaitá, em seis cursos;

150 vagas para o Instituto de Ciências Exatas e Tecnologia, em Itacoatiara, em dez cursos;

99 vagas para o Instituto de Ciências Sociais, Educação e Zootecnia (Icsez), em Parintins, em sete cursos.

Quem concluiu o ensino médio em escolas do interior do Amazonas, fora de Manaus, terá direito à Bonificação para o Interior (BI). No PSI 2027, o acréscimo será de 20% na nota, conforme portaria e resoluções da Ufam.

Para receber a bonificação, o candidato precisa:

Indicar a opção pela bonificação na inscrição.

Os documentos que comprovam a condição serão exigidos na matrícula.

Gabarito definitivo das provas: 9 de outubro de 2026

Resultado final: a partir 2 de dezembro de 2026

articles.title: Margot Robbie wore Elizabeth Taylor’s legendary 'Taj Mahal necklace' to a movie premiere: How did Mumtaz Mahal's necklace, gifted by Shah Jahan, reach Hollywood
articles.summary: Trending News: Margot Robbie has become one of the most watched names on any red carpet, for which fans wait with bated breath, leaving no occasion behind, be it a p.
articles.body: Margot Robbie has become one of the most watched names on any red carpet, for which fans wait with bated breath, leaving no occasion behind, be it a premiere or a press tour stop, to see what she'll wear next, whether it's a bold designer gown or something that represents the character she's playing. So when she stepped out for the Wuthering Heights premiere, all eyes were on her outfit as usual, except this time, the real showstopper wasn't the dress. It was the necklace around her neck.The Taj Mahal necklace has been passed down through empires, auction houses, and Hollywood marriages and carries more history in it than most museum pieces get credit for, but how did the jewel Margot Robbie chose to wear make its centuries-long journey from a Mughal empress to Hollywood?The story of the Taja mahal necklace that Margot Robbie wore at a movie premiereAt the Los Angeles premiere of Wuthering Heights this January, Margot Robbie showed up wearing something extraordinary that exudes Indian history: the legendary Taj Mahal diamond necklace that was once also owned by Elizabeth Taylor's, paired with a custom Schiaparelli gown.According to Forbes Australia, the heart-shaped diamond is mounted in jade and hangs from a custom gold, ruby, and diamond chain made by Cartier, styled to resemble the original silk cord the diamond hung from when it was first created for a Mughal emperor in the early 17th century.The pendant's surface carries an inscription in Parsee, translating to "Love is Everlasting," along with the name of Nur Jahan, the first woman to receive it as a gift from her husband, Jahangir..The stone's story actually begins centuries before Hollywood entered the pictureNur Jahan received the diamond from her husband, the Mughal Emperor Jahangir. It was later passed down to their son, Shah Jahan, who gifted it to his own wife, Mumtaz Mahal. When she died four years later, Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal as a monument to her memory, and the mausoleum eventually lent the diamond its name.The jewel's path into modern history runs through Cartier, which acquired it and had it remounted. The piece eventually made its way into the hands of Elizabeth Taylor's two-time husband, Richard Burton, "who presented it to Taylor in 1972 for her 40th birthday in Budapest." Burton had asked Cartier for gift ideas around Valentine's Day and Taylor's birthday, and secretly bought the necklace before surprising her with it during an elaborate birthday celebration.After Taylor passed away, the necklace was sold off as part of her estate auction. Forbes Australia reports it "was last sold to an anonymous buyer in 2011 for $8.8 million, breaking records for Indian jewels at the time," with the money from that sale going to the Elizabeth Taylor AIDS Foundation.But why did Margot Robbie choose to wear the necklace to the Wuthering Heights premiere?Burton had actually played Heathcliff himself, back in a 1958 TV version of the same book by Bronte, long before Robbie and Jacob Elordi stepped into the roles of Catherine and Heathcliff for this new version; it was just like a sweet, full-circle link back to Burton's own turn as Heathcliff.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry
articles.summary: The inquiry found a "complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit" where the nurse worked.
articles.body:
The public inquiry into how serial killer Lucy Letby was able to murder babies at the Countess of Chester hospital has delivered its findings, describing a "complete failure" to protect infants from harm.

After hearing from more than 130 witnesses, and considering 400 statements over six months, the Thirlwall Inquiry report was published earlier at Liverpool Town Hall.

The inquiry began in September 2024, after Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others - one of whom she attempted to kill twice.

Below are the key findings from Lady Justice Thirlwall's report, which ran to more than 1,100 pages over three volumes.

Hospital 'missed opportunities' to prevent murders

The first three deaths in June 2015 (babies A, C and D) were not viewed as a cluster of deaths, even though this was the annual number of deaths, concentrated into two weeks.

The fourth death, (Baby E) in August 2015, was unexpected and therefore reviewed at a serious incident panel meeting attended by the medical director and director of nursing - but it was treated as a formality.

"What is surprising is that no connection was made by any of the people involved to the earlier deaths," Thirlwall noted.

By August of that year, the total of four deaths was the highest since 2008, and was to double by the end of the year.

Thirlwall found that if a doctor – named in the report as Dr ZA - had not disregarded the insulin test result for Baby F in August 2015 then there should have been safeguarding action.

The safeguarding action would have prevented the attacks on babies G and H, J, K, L, M and N and the deaths of Baby I, O and P

If safeguarding action had been taken by October 2015 - after the death of Baby I - by moving Letby off the ward, the deaths of babies O and P would have been prevented, as would the attacks on babies J, K, L, M and N

In February 2016, Dr Ravi Jayaram should have reported what he had seen with regard to Baby K

In May 2016, no one raised safeguarding at a meeting with execs - if they had done it would have prevented the deaths of babies O and P

Thirlwall found there was a "complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit" at the Countess of Chester Hospital, where Letby, now 36, murdered seven babies and attempted to murder seven others, one of them twice.

She described a system of "dysfunctional management and governance".

Executives tried to 'control the narrative'

Thirlwall found hospital bosses repeatedly failed in their duty of candour with parents, investigators and regulators.

She added their behaviour was "high-handed, against all safeguarding principles, and foolhardy".

Medical director Ian Harvey "sought to control the narrative", and presented the case as he saw it.

He made sure that only documents that supported his case were seen, if necessary writing them himself.

Director of nursing Alison Kelly, the head of safeguarding, knew she had to act when there was a suspicion that a baby had been harmed, and others might be at risk – but did not

Chief executive Tony Chambers was dictatorial in his approach to consultants, and executive presentations to the hospital's board were an "exercise in spin"

He added to the unnecessary delay in contacting police

His intention throughout was to stall or obstruct the police investigation, which he succeeded in doing for almost a year

The report was critical of a raft of internal and external reviews commissioned by hospital leadership after concerns were raised about Letby

Director of nursing for urgent care Karen Rees had "lost all judgement" and had a "hostile approach", Thirlwall found.

She also found that unit manager Eirian Powell's judgement "was affected by the view that Letby was a very good nurse".

'Toxic negativity' towards whistleblowers

Thirwall found wider NHS failings played their part, with a tendency across the health service for management to become pre-occupied with avoiding blame and focusing on reputation management.

She said there was still a "toxic negativity" that discouraged people within the NHS from speaking out, even though efforts had been made over the last decade to strengthen protections for whistleblowers.

Regulation was also found to be lacking.

The Care Quality Commission (CQC) inspected the Countess of Chester in February 2016 but Letby carried on attacking babies until June of that year.

Key information was withheld from inspectors, but the regulator was criticised for not showing enough curiosity to look beyond what it was being told, even though the CQC had been warned by the inquiry into baby deaths at Morecambe Bay NHS Trust that it needed to take a tougher approach.

Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented

Repeatedly untruthful, callous and quiet - what we learned about Lucy Letby from inquiry report

As it happened: Read the live coverage from the Thirlwall Inquiry

The parents of babies were "kept in the dark for years" over concerns that their children may have been deliberately harmed.

Thirlwall found their treatment to be "reprehensible", and said hospital executives used the risk of upsetting the parents as a convenient argument to justify not calling the police.

In relation to the treatment of doctors, she said it should "never have been about nurses against doctors… it was about keeping babies safe".

Doctors were found not to have been given the protection of the Speak Out Safely whistleblowing policy, and senior managers tried to "manage out" consultants, and suggested they might be referred to the General Medical Council watchdog.

Allegations first described as 'witch hunt'

Letby took out a grievance against the hospital in 2017, after being moved off her normal duties amid allegations about her.

The report found that "the way Letby's grievance and its consequences were handled was deplorable", adding that the investigating officer in charge "could bring neither independence nor objectivity to it".

The evidence of Alison Kelly and Ian Harvey was found to be "factually inaccurate and misleading", and the chair of the governance panel, Annette Weatherly, was "unfair in her approach", having initially described the allegations against Letby as a "witch hunt".

Letby falsified records and ignored instructions

Police were called into the hospital in 2017.

Thirlwall added "no-one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm - and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt".

She said safeguarding guidance "makes no difference" if "those to whom concerns are expressed do nothing".

The report found Letby had ignored management instructions when she disliked them and shouted at her manager.

She had falsified records and one infant in her care had been found covered in their own faeces.

She was also found to have been repeatedly untruthful in her dealings with friends and colleagues, and was noted by patients to have been "inappropriate" and "callous" in her manner.

Access to insulin 'should be restricted'

Thirlwall made 17 recommendations in her report, which ran to over 1,100 pages over three volumes.

She said that cots and incubators in neonatal units should be fitted with baby monitors, and access to insulin - which Letby was convicted of administering to two of the babies she killed - should be controlled by either biometric data or CCTV monitoring.

She also said a "suspicion of deliberate harm" policy, which outlines the steps to be taken by managers when suspicions are raised, needed to be created, and that NHS staff should be contractually obligated to follow the policy and other safeguarding guidance.

articles.title: $33.4bn war cost, $22.3bn on munitions: What US lost in 6 months of Iran war
articles.summary: International News: The United States has suffered extensive losses to aircraft, military facilities and diplomatic infrastructure during its war with Iran, while a Penta.
articles.body: The United States has suffered extensive losses to aircraft, military facilities and diplomatic infrastructure during its war with Iran, while a Pentagon watchdog has warned that the conflict has also exposed shortages in advanced munitions and bottlenecks in the US defence supply chain.A US Department of Defense inspector general report released Monday provided the first official accounting of the damage from the conflict, covering the period from February 28 to June 30. The report said Iranian strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US military installations across eight countries, while dozens of American aircraft and drones were damaged or destroyed.The report also found that the war had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”, raising questions over Washington's ability to sustain a prolonged high-intensity conflict.The findings come even as President Donald Trump has pushed back against reports of dwindling US weapons stocks. In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump said the US was producing and delivering advanced weapons to American forces in the Middle East.“I’ve just received a report that the United States is producing more exquisite and elite weapons than at any time in our history. They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East and beyond,” Trump wrote.How much has Iran war cost US?The Pentagon watchdog estimated that about $22 billion was spent on munitions between February 28 and June 30 during Operation Epic Fury, the US military's name for the campaign.The broader cost of the war was estimated at about $33 billion during the same period, according to the report. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had separately told Congress in July that the war had cost $37.5 billion.The report's assessment provides a broader picture of the financial and operational burden on the US military after months of strikes involving American and Israeli forces on one side and Iran on the other.Trump says US weapons production is surgingTrump has repeatedly rejected reports that the US military is facing shortages of key weapons.“Our defense company factories are moving 24/7 while at the same time, building, on average 4-to-5 large-scale brand-new plants, each. A primary focus of this production has been Patriots, THAAD systems, Tomahawks and other standard missile systems, of which we already have large numbers in stock,” Trump wrote.However, the Pentagon inspector general's report acknowledged shortages in advanced munitions and problems in replenishing stocks.A separate analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies found that US stocks of some critical missile interceptors had fallen sharply during the conflict.As of July 27, the US was estimated to have between 759 and 827 Patriot interceptors, down from about 2,330 before the war. THAAD interceptors had fallen to between 234 and 278, compared with 452 before the conflict.The Pentagon has moved to increase production. It signed a deal with Northrop Grumman to expand production of THAAD and Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors, although new systems could take years to become available.Dozens of US aircraft and drones damaged or destroyedThe watchdog report documented losses across a wide range of US aircraft, including fighter jets, refuelling tankers, surveillance aircraft and helicopters.At least four F-15E fighter jets were destroyed. Three were shot down by friendly fire over Kuwait on March 1, while another was lost during combat over Iran in April. All aircrews were recovered.At least one F-35A stealth fighter was damaged by Iranian fire, while at least one A-10 ground-attack aircraft was shot down.The US also lost or damaged at least seven KC-135 aerial refuelling tankers. One crashed in Iraq during a refuelling mission, while five others were damaged on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian missiles and drones.At least one E-3 Sentry airborne early-warning aircraft was damaged at Saudi Arabia's Prince Sultan Air Base. An HH-60W helicopter was also damaged during a combat search and rescue mission.The losses extended to unmanned systems. At least one MQ-4C Triton surveillance aircraft crashed, while four AH-6 helicopters were destroyed after being deemed unrecoverable during a combat search and rescue operation.At least one AH-64 Apache attack helicopter was shot down near the Strait of Hormuz on June 8. An MH-60S helicopter later crashed in the Arabian Sea on July 1.The largest reported loss involved the MQ-9 Reaper, with as many as 30 drones destroyed.417 US military personnel woundedThe Pentagon report said the US military recorded at least 11 personnel killed in action during the conflict, while seven others died in non-hostile incidents.At least 417 US service members were wounded in Iranian attacks through June 30.Some of the deaths occurred during Iranian strikes on US positions in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Iraq. Other fatalities resulted from aircraft accidents classified as non-hostile incidents.Iran strikes damaged US bases across eight countriesIranian attacks damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan, according to the watchdog.The report did not provide a total cost for the damage to US military facilities.One of the most consequential attacks targeted the US Navy's regional logistics hub in Bahrain, forcing the military to shift personnel, assets, storage facilities and supply lines to alternative locations.The disruption was severe enough for Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean to become an important logistics hub. The report said the shift resulted in 14-to-18-day logistics cycles for some supplies.The report also said establishing adequate naval bases and support ports posed challenges because of uncertainties over host-nation access and logistical arrangements.US diplomatic facilities suffered $184 million damageIranian attacks also damaged US diplomatic facilities in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, with the combined damage estimated at $184 million.Iraq accounted for the largest share. The US mission reported more than 600 attacks through the end of June, with damage estimated at nearly $157 million.The US Consulate General in Erbil suffered damage to multiple buildings, while the US Embassy in Baghdad and the Baghdad Diplomatic Support Center were also hit.In Kuwait, the US Embassy suspended operations in March following attacks and damage to its facilities, resulting in an estimated cost of nearly $14.75 million.Two Iranian drones struck the US Embassy compound in Riyadh on March 3, causing damage estimated at about $11.5 million. The US Consulate General in Dubai also sustained damage to a utility building.Thousands of US diplomatic personnel displacedThe conflict also disrupted US diplomatic operations across the region.Up to 3,500 diplomatic personnel were outside the region between February 23 and June 30, with several US diplomatic posts placed under authorised or ordered departure.The US also evacuated around 9,000 American citizens from countries across the Middle East and Europe after the conflict began. The State Department said its evacuation operations had cost more than $11 million by late June.The report comes as Washington weighs the longer-term impact of the conflict on its military posture in the Middle East, including whether some reductions in US personnel and facilities could become permanent.

articles.title: UN considers underground aid bunkers in Ukraine as Russian strikes escalate
articles.summary: Europe News: The United Nations is considering moving humanitarian aid supplies underground in Ukraine to protect them from Russian strikes, the UN humanitarian co.
articles.body: The United Nations is considering moving humanitarian aid supplies underground in Ukraine to protect them from Russian strikes, the UN humanitarian coordinator said on Tuesday.The strikes have hit 10 UN warehouses this year, destroying supplies worth millions of dollars.“These deliberate attacks on warehousing capacities, is a new trend of the last few months,” UN humanitarian coordinator in Ukraine Matthias Schmale told Reuters in Geneva after briefing states on Ukraine’s humanitarian needs in the fifth year since Russia’s full-scale invasion.He said the organisation was considering moving aid supplies into underground bunkers and delaying purchases until the last possible moment to minimise their exposure to strikes.“This feels increasingly like the front line is moving into the air,” he said. “That means extra cost also to the taxpayers, who at the end of the day pay for the goods that the U.N. and other humanitarians bring in,” he added, noting that such additional costs had not been factored into the UN’s $2.3 billion aid budget for 2026.Schmale said one of the World Health Organization’s main warehouses containing medical supplies was hit earlier this month, while other strikes destroyed hygiene kits and school supplies for children.He said the UN was investing in equipment to protect staff, including additional armoured vehicles and drone-detection devices.The organisation is also considering expanding support for Ukrainian requests for mobile drone shelters in public areas, such as near bus stops, as civilian casualties continue to rise.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A TikTok reviewer stopped at an overlooked Anime NYC booth; his video drew 1 million likes, gave indie creator Dare 25,000 followers and sold out his comics overnight
articles.summary: US News: A TikTok reviewer who makes a habit of stopping at comic convention booths that attract little attention ended up giving an indie comic creator a majo.
articles.body: A TikTok reviewer who makes a habit of stopping at comic convention booths that attract little attention ended up giving an indie comic creator a major boost after visiting his stall at Anime NYC. The reviewer, known online as @slow_comics, posted a video about Dare and his comics, and the video went viral with one million likes. The exposure brought about 25,000 new followers to Dare’s creator account and helped him sell out his available copies almost overnight.@slow_comics has built a following of about 40,000 on TikTok through his own comic series and his convention visits where he looks for booths that other visitors appear to be overlooking, Good News Network reported. That led him to Dare, an American of Nigerian heritage who was publishing and illustrating an independent comic inspired by his Yoruba heritage.The main comic, “Ori: Holder of the Heads”, follows a world where people can speak to their ancestors and ask them for advice. However, the story takes a darker turn when the ancestors begin attacking people. The main characters then try to understand what has happened and why the attacks have started.The reviewer was particularly taken by the comic’s artwork, colours and use of African cloth patterns in the backgrounds and textures. He also praised the story concept and another comic by Dare called “Etch”. Unlike a conventional comic, “Etch” can be read in both directions, with each reading direction presenting a different perspective in an argument between two strange creatures.TikTok video brings a surge of interest@slow_comics posted about the comics after buying them at Anime NYC. In his video, he described himself as “ecstatic” about the purchase and said he was excited to read the books. The video attracted one million likes and quickly sent new viewers towards Dare’s creator account.The response had a direct effect on Dare’s sales. About 25,000 people followed his account after the video went viral, and they began buying the remaining copies of “Ori”. The limited presale was also sold out.The demand became so high that Dare had to call on his brother, Joshua, to help bring more physical copies from Pennsylvania to New York. Those copies were also sold out.In a follow-up video, Dare thanked the community for the support and explained how interested readers and collectors could get the next editions of his comics.The reviewer later posted another video confirming the popularity of the comics. “I can confirm that Etch and Ori are just as good as you think they’re going to be,” @slow_comics said. “Due to the virality of the video, he sold out basically overnight.”Comics draw on Yoruba heritageDare’s work is rooted in his Nigerian heritage, with “Ori: Holder of the Heads” using that cultural background as part of its story and visual style. The comic centres on characters trying to understand their relationship with ancestors after those ancestors begin attacking people.The reviewer highlighted the use of African cloth patterns in the backgrounds and textures of the comic. He also pointed to the details in the artwork, including the way textures were used in elements such as tree bark.“Etch” takes a different approach. It can be read from left to right or right to left, and the direction changes the perspective of an argument between two creatures. The story also includes a “trickster” character, an element the reviewer said was among his favourite parts of the comic.The creator and his comics were next scheduled to appear at the Small Press Expo in Bethesda, Maryland, on September 12 and 13. Dare is also scheduled to take part in the Uhuru Book Fair at Clark Park in Philadelphia the following weekend.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Poland reinforces border with Ukraine amid growing security concerns across Europe
articles.summary: Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz announced Tuesday that the country is reinforcing security at its border with Ukraine after Russian drone strikes near crossings heightened concerns among NATO allies.
articles.body: Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz announced Tuesday that the country is reinforcing security at its border with Ukraine after Russian drone strikes near crossings heightened concerns among NATO allies. “Recent days show that ‌Russia’s actions ⁠threaten the security of all of Europe. In accordance with our government’s decision, the infrastructure used by the Border Guard is being strengthened,” Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X following the two weekend strikes, one of which hit a train as a group of former Western officials were traveling in the area. “Soldiers of the 18th Engineer Regiment are ‌already carrying out tasks, thanks to which the checkpoints and infrastructure near the Polish-Ukrainian border will ⁠be reinforced.” The Russian Ministry of Defense on Tuesday confirmed two strikes near the Polish border, claiming the train had been transporting military cargo. Earlier Tuesday, military officials in Lithuania, another NATO member, said a drone had been shot down in the country’s airspace for the first time. The drone was equipped with an explosive device, which was neutralized by bomb disposal experts, according to the Lithuanian Ministry of Defense. An investigation is ongoing to determine the origin of the drone, the ministry told CNN. Italy’s defense minister, Guido Crosetto, said an Italian NATO fighter jet shot down the drone, adding that it “most probably came from Russia.” The Italian Defense Ministry said in a statement that it was the second incident involving the country’s fighter jets in the space of a month. “It is also because of incidents like this that the presence of our military on the Eastern Flank is crucial for ensuring communitarian security,” Crosetto said. Also on Tuesday, the Danish Armed Forces said a Danish military helicopter was targeted by a Russian warship, which fired two emergency flares while the helicopter was taking routine photographs of the vessel in international waters on Monday. Following the incident, Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha expressed support for Denmark “in the wake of Russia’s provocative and unacceptable action.” “Moscow continues its attempts to destabilize Europe, not just Denmark,” he added in a post on X, calling for joint and decisive action to protect Europe from Russian threats. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Monday that strikes close to NATO territory reflected Russian President Vladimir Putin’s “desperation” and his desire “to sow fear and terror.” Rutte has pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance’s defenses along its border with Russia and its close ally Belarus. Meanwhile, the United States appears to be working to stop Ukraine and Russia from hitting each other’s energy targets amid concerns over the global spike in fuel prices. US President Donald Trump said on Monday that the countries agreed to halt energy-related attacks, but both his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky and the Kremlin later described it as a proposal rather than a firm agreement. Ukraine has been hammering Russian fuel infrastructure for months, severely reducing Moscow’s refining capacity and triggering widespread supply shortages. In response, Russia has banned the foreign sale of its diesel. “There is now a strong US proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure,” Zelensky said on Monday night. “If this can become the first de-escalatory step – a step toward ending Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response – then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation.” CNN’s Lauren Kent and Stefano Pozzebon contributed to this report

articles.title: More than 100,000 displaced as they flee violence in Yemen: UN
articles.summary: Thousands making risky maritime journey to Djibouti as conflict between Yemen gov’t and Houthis intensifies.
articles.body:
More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee the conflict in Yemen between the Houthis and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, according to the United Nations.

The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) said in a statement issued on Tuesday that the rapidly escalating hostilities along Yemen’s western coast have displaced more than 100,000 people inside the country, and forced thousands more to risk the dangerous journey across the Bab al-Mandeb strait to reach Djibouti in search of safety.

The UNHCR statement warned that the violence threatens to trigger a humanitarian crisis, as more people are displaced, pressuring communities with limited resources.

The agency said it requires an estimated $14m in new funding to meet the immediate needs of displaced families inside Yemen, with additional support needed for those arriving in Djibouti.

“Many families fled at short notice with few belongings. Shelter, food, clean water, health care and protection services are among the most urgent needs, as receiving communities and displacement sites become overstretched,” the statement reads.

More than 65,000 registered refugees and asylum seekers inside Yemen, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia, are also facing risks due to the fighting.

The displacement began when the Iran-aligned Houthis began a rapid advance , seizing control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coast to cement their grip on Bab al-Mandeb.

The strategic waterway is a critical maritime corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and has become an alternative shipping route as the United States’ war against Iran choked the Strait of Hormuz.

Aisha Muhammad, a displaced woman, had to leave her five children in their village near the port city of Mocha when it was overrun by the Houthis last week.

“They are being blocked and shot at, so they are trapped inside their homes. They are cooking only rice, no bread, nothing else. My daughters called me saying they want to join us, but it has become too difficult,” said Muhammad.

Hussein Haydara, a displaced man from Hodeidah, said he was forced to escape suddenly with his family.

“You could barely take your children and the fewest essentials with you,” he said. “We were terrified of the shelling and sniper fire, and you just flee as quickly as you can out of fear for your children and your family.”

UNHCR reports that more than 2,400 people made the journey across the Bab al-Mandeb strait in the past four days. Most arrivals are women, children and older people, it said.

“People are arriving after a difficult sea journey, many exhausted, distressed and carrying what little they could take with them,” Sandrine Desamours, UNHCR’s representative in Djibouti, said.
