articles.title: Skyrocketing fuel prices spark protests around the globe
articles.summary: Protesters are taking to the streets around the world to voice anger about skyrocketing fuel prices and rolling blackouts, as the war in Iran drives up the cost of energy.
articles.body: Protesters are taking to the streets around the world to voice anger about skyrocketing fuel prices and rolling blackouts, as the war in Iran drives up the cost of energy. Oil prices climbed back above the $100 per barrel mark last week in the wake of further US strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf and reignited fighting in Yemen that threatens shipping in the Bab al-Mandab Strait. For the United States, that has meant elevated gas prices and stark warnings for households that rely on heating oil to keep warm in the winter, as analysts forecast a 30% jump in prices amid the Iran war. As the price of fuel ratchets up, so does the anger of people who can no longer afford to pay for gas, get to work, run their businesses or even carry out essential services. In Syria, protesters burned tires on a busy highway. In Guatemala, they blocked roads to demand immediate government action. And in Portugal, local business leaders and workers marched to the prime minister’s home. Here’s a closer look at the protests and the global impacts of sky-high energy costs: Syria A steep rise in fuel prices over the weekend ignited protests across Syria, marking the largest demonstrations in the country since the fall of the Assad regime two years ago. The country’s government temporarily raised diesel prices to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.43) a liter – roughly a 40% hike – according to Syrian news agency SANA. It also raised prices for gas by more than 25%. The Syrian Energy Ministry has said the steep price increases are due to surging global fuel prices and ongoing maintenance at the country’s largest refinery, Baniyas, which has increased its reliance on imports, SANA reported. While dozens of protests have been peaceful, demonstrators on Sunday blocked the Hasaka–Deir ez-Zor highway, where they burned tires and stopped oil tankers, according to ACLED, a global conflict monitor. “Fuel availability, rising prices, falling purchasing power, and poor services are all reasons that have accumulated public resentment, although demands are also shifting toward reversing decisions and removing officials, including the energy minister, showing that economic grievances are turning into grievances against the government,” said Muaz Al Abdullah, a Syria analyst at ACLED. Video filmed by Reuters news agency from the scene of a protest in Aleppo on Sunday shows people burning tires and shouting chants criticizing the governments’ fuel hike decision. “All those present here want a reduction in diesel prices. We don’t want higher wages, we want cheaper (fuel),” one Syrian protester, Yasser Salim, told Reuters. Another protester, Bassam al-Ali, said: “We do not want roundabouts, every day they (the government) build a new roundabout that costs a million thousand dollars, and malls and I don’t know what … Your people were with you, is still with you now and will remain with you – but this will let things explode.” Guatemala Last week in Guatemala, groups of organized truckers and other protesters blocked highways and caused damage in various parts of the country to protest rising fuel prices, according to the Associated Press. Other videos taken by local media show people marching peacefully through Guatemala City to demand immediate government action. The country’s Congress is now working to address the widespread discontent through a proposed law that would cap prices until the end of the year, but the bill is still making its way through the legislative process, according to Guatemala’s national news agency AGN. If passed, it would mean that a government subsidy is paid to fuel importers if prices exceed the established cap, according to AP. “This is an issue that must be resolved as a country. The executive, the legislative, and everyone else involved must resolve it. People cannot pay these prices and not feel the impact on their finances,” said the president of the Congress, Luis Contreras Colindres, in an address on Monday. “Diesel is the engine that drives this country’s economy,” Contreras said, according to AGN. Portugal Protests took place in the coastal city of Espinho, Portugal, on Saturday to protest both rising gas prices and the soaring cost of living. About 80 people took part in that demonstration, which was organized by local business leaders and aimed at pressuring the government to find solutions, according to Portugal’s Lusa News Agency. The protesters marched until they reached the home of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro in Espinho. Meanwhile, the Portuguese Firefighters’ League (LBP) has sounded the alarm that surging fuel prices are becoming unsustainable for fire brigades and saddling volunteer organizations with costs they can’t keep up with. On Monday, the country’s government announced a new package of measures intended to ease the fuel price crunch, according to Lusa. Those measures include support for freight transporters, taxi drivers, the fire service and the social sector, the news agency reported. CNN’s Heather Law contributed to this report.

articles.title: Pennsylvania officials report fourth measles-associated death in 'surge' of cases
articles.summary: The US has this year experienced the highest number of deaths from the virus since the 1990s.
articles.body:
A fourth person has died from complications related to measles in Pennsylvania, say state officials, in an outbreak that has infected hundreds of people.

An 18-year-old died from acute encephalomyelitis, a rare and severe neurological complication of measles, the Mifflin County Coroner's Office in Pennsylvania said.

The Keystone state has seen over 600 cases of measles this year, primarily in Lancaster County.

The US eliminated measles in 2000 with the help of vaccines, but it has this year experienced the highest number of deaths from the virus since the 1990s.

Last year, three people - including two children - died from a measles outbreak in Texas that spread predominantly among the Mennonite community.

The rising number of cases has come as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates.

In Pennsylvania, state and local officials have said the 18-year-old and a 40-year-old - both unvaccinated - died from measles-related complications over the past month.

Two infants have also died. US children typically do not receive their first MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine until 12 months of age.

The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented.

The highly contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia.

To achieve herd immunity, around 95% of the population must have the vaccine, say health officials.

Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro posted on X on Tuesday: "This disease was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 - yet decades later, we are seeing it surge due to lower vaccination rates."

The reporting of the deaths in Pennsylvania has led to tensions between Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.

Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about vaccines and has said he would withhold information about the deaths from the top health official in order to protect the families of the deceased.

Kennedy has questioned whether the infant deaths were in fact from measles.

A 40-year-old woman died in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania, on Saturday, with the coroner saying the cause of death was respiratory failure due to measles.

Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni said a six-week-old born with a rare genetic condition, Amish lethal microcephaly, died of measles on 18 August.

Diamantoni has said another infant who tested positive for measles died soon after birth on 14 August, with the primary cause of death listed as a spleen laceration.

Measles infections can cause the spleen to enlarge, raising the risk of rupture. State health officials have said the death was from a measles infection that resulted in a spleen rupture.

In a post on X after the first two deaths in the state, Kennedy accused Shapiro of "political grandstanding".

The health secretary said the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would only update its information on deaths once reviews were complete.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it had conducted "rigorous investigations" with the coroner's offices to confirm that the latest two deaths were indeed from measles.

"These investigations included confirming clinical evidence of a measles infection, a positive laboratory test, and that the death was not due to an unrelated cause," the health department said.

In November, a panel is set to decide whether the US will lose its status of having eliminated measles, which Canada lost last year.

Kennedy has been criticised by public health experts who argue his remarks and remaking of US vaccine policy has hindered efforts to stop the outbreaks.

A vaccine sceptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the MMR vaccine, which has proven safe and effective.

The health secretary has said the worsening measles outbreak is a global problem.

Speaking before a Senate committee last month, he said: "A lot of nations have lost their elimination status. The whole world had their worst measles year."

articles.title: 'One in, one out' scheme costs £56,000 per migrant, home secretary says
articles.summary: Shabana Mahmood says the policy has been "difficult" to scale up and the numbers involved are still "relatively small".
articles.body:
The government's "one in, one out" scheme to send migrants who cross the Channel back to France costs on average £56,000 per person, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has said.

That is higher than the Home Office's estimated average cost for enforced migrant returns of £48,800.

The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.

Mahmood told MPs the policy had been "difficult" to scale up and the numbers involved were still "relatively small".

She said the total number deported under the scheme since it began in August 2025 was around 1,400.

Asked by the Conservative MP Robbie Moore whether she thought the scheme had been a success, Mahmood said: "On its own terms, can you prove the concept that such a deal is viable, that you can get returns off and up and running - yes.

"It's not been without its challenges, obviously. The numbers are still relatively small.

"What has been more operationally difficult is to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system."

She said the UN and other agencies had reported that some migrants were not getting on small boats because they thought there was a chance they could be accepted under the "one in, one out" scheme.

Fall in small boats down to law enforcement, agency says

The agreement aims to deter people from making the dangerous journey across the Channel.

It had been due to end in June 2026 but has now been extended into October.

Asked how much the policy was costing, Mahmood said she thought it was "about £56,000" but added that she would write to the committee to confirm the figure.

So far this year, 17,425 people have arrived in the UK by small boat, a 44% decrease compared to the same time last year.

The National Crime Agency has said law enforcement had been a "key factor" in getting the numbers down.

It also said supply chains for small boats had been disrupted by the war in the Middle East.

articles.title: Mounted police, extra patrols and Kiffin hate: Oxford prepares for Ole Miss-LSU game with extra security
articles.summary: Lane Kiffin's return to Oxford as LSU head coach prompted unprecedented security measures, with multiple police departments sending crowd-control units.
articles.body: It’s been building for ten months, and Lane Kiffin’s return to Oxford is finally here. The former Ole Miss head coach will officially return to town Saturday afternoon as LSU’s head coach, and the city is making sure every security measure is in place. Usually, this would be just another weekend of SEC football in the South. Parties in the 'Grove,' fans enjoying the tailgate scene, bars overflowing into the streets as supporters keep themselves lubricated during the day and the police department only dealing with a smaller number of problems. ELLA LANGLEY, DISTRACTIONS AND LANE KIFFIN: PETE GOLDING CALLS OLE MISS-LSU 'HIGH SCHOOL HOMECOMING' But, this is obviously not just another game-day in Oxford for the police department. The built-up frustration over the offseason storylines surrounding Lane Kiffin will finally reach a boiling point before Saturday even arrives. I don't think folks are underselling the amount of vitriol that will be spewed towards the former Ole Miss head coach when lamenting over the stories created over the past ten months. Also, this won't be Kiffin's first time back in Oxford since his departure, as he has visited numerous times, even taking in a few yoga classes in the process. His daughter, Landry, still attends Ole Miss, though most of her time is spent in Baton Rouge with boyfriend Whit Weeks. He just also happens to be LSU's starting linebacker, which I'm sure leads to some interesting conversations at practice between him and Kiffin. But, this weekend is all about a return to the city that put Lane back on the map, and they are waiting for him. Security measures have been planned for months, with LSU heading to town This was not a process created by the local town hall during a weekly meeting. The amount of police, state patrol, federal law enforcement and out-of-state help that will be roaming Oxford this weekend should make for a pretty safe day in terms of fan behavior. One would think, at least. On Tuesday morning, the Mobile, Alabama, police department confirmed they are sending their crowd-control units to Oxford for the weekend. "The Mobile Police Department’s Mounted Unit will be in Oxford, MS from Thursday, September 17th – Saturday, September 19th working with local law enforcement during the area’s upcoming event," a spokesperson said in a statement. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE In addition to the help from Mobile, the City of New Orleans will also be sending its mounted police to the Ole Miss campus this weekend to provide help with crowd control. Also, sources tell OutKick that there will be additional support for the LSU football team, with Louisiana State Patrol sending additional members to Oxford, more than usual for a road game. You can expect a large amount of security around Lane Kiffin at all times this weekend, while the school will also take measures to not give out where the team is staying on the night before Saturday's showdown. Ole Miss' Pete Golding implores fans to welcome opposing fans Look, there is no love lost between LSU and the Rebels. Lost in the chaos of Lane Kiffin returning is the fact that these two teams have a storied history in the 'Magnolia Bowl', and there is plenty of hatred already instilled between these fans. But, that doesn’t mean Pete Golding isn’t imploring his fans to use that Southern hospitality at its finest. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "To me, what this place has always been about, why so many people love coming here and respect this place is because of the people who are here and how they make (other fans) feel when they come here. Be there early and be loud," Pete Golding noted. "But I think at the end of the day, there’s still a respect piece. And this place has always been known to have really, really good people. Let’s not lose that over a game or a person or anything like that." As for Lane Kiffin, he seemed pretty content with the fact he is playing the villain, which actually takes the attention off his football team, and puts the pressure on Ole Miss. "I guess there’s real safety issues and stuff, so there’s people that have a plan for that," Kiffin mentioned. "I told the players today, ‘Man, you don’t have anything to worry about as far as, like, attention on you all week and everything. There’s going to be so much attention, hatred, everything on me. You just get to go play. Really, the pressure’s on them." OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD That's one way to look at it. articles.title: Magazine from 1894 is finally returned to New Hampshire public library
articles.summary: A magazine, checked out and overdue from a New Hampshire library, has finally been returned — perhaps as long as 132 years late.
articles.body: A magazine, checked out and overdue from a New Hampshire library, has finally been returned — perhaps as long as 132 years late. John Hanson, an 84-year-old Barrington resident, recently strolled into the Concord Public Library to turn in a relatively well cared for edition of “The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine” from September of 1894. In theory, Hanson could’ve been on the hook for a $12,055 fine for being 48,220 days overdue. But when Hanson returned it, the library was in the midst of a “fine freeze,” which canceled late fees. “Yeah, when I saw that, I said to myself, ‘Boy, this would be a good time to bring it back,’” Hanson told NBC News on Tuesday. The magazine is clearly the property of the Concord Public Library with a bookplate bearing its name and a reminder to readers that this periodical “may be kept for one week.” Archivist and outreach coordinator Jennifer Needham was working at the circulation desk when Hanson arrived with an envelope in hand. “‘I have a book to return and I bet you haven’t seen anything like this,’” Needham said, recalling Hanson’s introduction. “I honestly thought it was going to be from the 1980s, 90s, or 2000s. But then he pulled this out and I was like ‘Ooo tell me more!’ ” Hanson, a Concord native, said he first came upon the periodical during a move from Boscawen to Barrington in 1966. He didn’t know then, and still doesn’t know now, how the work got into his possession. His parents didn’t have Concord Public Library cards, he said. Hanson’s late, first wife Carol was a voracious reader and frequent Concord Public Library patron. But he insisted that she, more than anyone else, wouldn’t have allowed a checked out book or magazine to languish for so many years. “I don’t know, I really don’t know (how the book came into his possession),” Hanson said. “So I don’t know if it’s something that I got as a gift that was given to me. Or did I pick this up from a pile of free books on the side of the road to read? I honestly don’t know.” The periodical was typical of its time with a wide variety of writings that included poetry, essays and news. One topical story in that edition that caught Needham’s eye was about the rise of playgrounds at urban public schools. “That’s one thing that was really interesting,” the librarian said. “I didn’t know this history, that they were arguing that more city schools should have outdoor spaces for children to play. It sounds like during that time, that just wasn’t a priority. It’s interesting that they would play inside then.”
